facts.t: India is a Union of States, never a federation
facts.d: Article 1 deliberately avoids the word federation. Ambedkar explained the choice: the Union is not the result of an agreement between states, and no state has the right to secede from it — unlike the American compact.

The end of single-party dominance that year put opposition governments in nine states at once. Almost every federal controversy since — Governors, Article 356, finance commissions, inter-state councils — traces back to that break.

facts.t: Entry 97 is the catch-all that never empties
facts.d: Residuary powers sit with Parliament through Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List. In the United States and Australia residuary power lies with the states; India followed the Canadian model instead, which is a large part of why Wheare called the system quasi-federal.

bank.q: Who described the Indian Constitution as quasi-federal?
bank.e: K. C. Wheare. Alexandrowicz went further and questioned whether India should be called a federation at all; Granville Austin preferred cooperative federalism.

bank.q: With reference to the distribution of legislative powers, consider the following statements:
s: Residuary powers vest exclusively in Parliament under Article 248.
In the Concurrent field, state law prevails over Union law in case of repugnancy.
Parliament may make laws having extra-territorial operation.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Article 254 provides that Union law prevails on repugnancy in the Concurrent field — the reverse of statement 2.

bank.q: Match List I (article) with List II (subject):
pairs: 1. Repugnancy between Union and State laws
3. Extent of laws made by Parliament and State legislatures
4. Distribution of subjects across the three Lists
bank.e: Article 245 concerns territorial extent, 246 the three Lists, 248 residuary power, and 254 repugnancy.

bank.q: The number of subjects in the Union, State and Concurrent Lists respectively is:
bank.e: 97 Union, 66 State and 47 Concurrent subjects as originally framed — the figures shift slightly with amendments, but these are the standard numbers.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT a correct statement of the doctrine of territorial nexus?
o: The connection must be real and not illusory
The liability imposed must be pertinent to the connection
The nexus theory itself imposes the tax
Extra-territorial laws must have a nexus with something in India
bank.e: Tata Steel v. State of Bihar clarified that nexus theory does not impose a tax — it merely indicates the circumstances in which a tax may be enforced.

bank.as: Federalism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
bank.rs: The Centre cannot amend India into a unitary state.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion. Kesavananda and S. R. Bommai both list federalism among the basic features precisely because it places the Union–State distribution beyond the reach of the amending power.

bank.q: Consider the following statements about the 2024 mineral-royalty rulings:
s: States can collect royalty on major minerals.
States can additionally tax major minerals.
bank.e: All three are correct, and together they open a significant revenue channel for the states — an unusual recent expansion of state fiscal space.

bank.q: In State of Bihar v. Charusila Das (1959) the Court held that a State may legislate on trusts within its territory:
o: Only if all trust property lies within the State
Even if some trust property lies in another State
Only with the prior consent of the other State
Only where the trust is registered under central law
bank.e: The nexus was the trust's situation within the State; the location of some of its property elsewhere did not defeat the State's competence.

bank.q: All of the following support the description of India as a strong-Centre federation EXCEPT:
o: Union law prevailing in the Concurrent field
Parliament legislating for Union Territories without legislatures
States being able to tax major minerals
bank.e: That is a recent expansion of state power, running against the strong-Centre grain rather than supporting it.

bank.q: Arrange the following in correct chronological order:
items: End of one-party dominance in the states
bank.e: State of Bombay v. RMDC (1957) → the end of one-party dominance (1967) → Electronics Corporation v. CIT (1989) → S. R. Bommai (1994).

bank.q: With reference to Article 245, consider the following statements:
s: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of the territory of India.
A State legislature may legislate for the whole or any part of that State.
A law of Parliament is invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 245(2) expressly provides that no Parliamentary law shall be deemed invalid on the ground of extra-territorial operation.
